--- title: "Lesson 22 · Bayesian regression and GLMs" subtitle: "Part V · Bayesian modeling" description: "Bayesian logistic regression, priors for regression coefficients, answering questions with posterior draws, posterior predictive checks, and reporting a Bayesian analysis." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 8, 12 and 19–21]{} [Threads: likelihood · uncertainty · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - fit a Bayesian logistic regression and compare it with the frequentist fit; - choose weakly informative priors for regression coefficients on the odds ratio scale; - answer substantive questions, including causal contrasts, by computing on posterior draws; - check a model's fit with posterior predictive checks, and recognize overdispersion; - report a Bayesian analysis completely. ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** This is where Lessons 8 and 19–21 meet. The models are the same GLMs; the Bayesian version adds priors and returns draws. The draws make two things easy that are awkward otherwise: probability statements about effects ("how likely is it that the OR exceeds 1.1?"), and uncertainty for derived quantities such as the cases prevented by an intervention (Lesson 12). ::: ## 22.1 Bayesian logistic regression {#s1} The NO₂–asthma model of Lesson 8, with priors. Each 10 µg/m³ gets a prior on its log odds ratio; the adjustment variables get weakly informative priors too. With the full cohort, the prior barely matters. With a small sample, it does. Move the sample size and the prior, and compare the posterior with the frequentist estimate. ```{=html}
priorfrequentist estimate and 95% CIposterior
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$Y_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_i), \qquad \mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = \alpha + \beta\,\frac{\mathrm{NO}_{2,i}}{10} + \gamma^\top z_i$$ $$\beta \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 0.5^2), \quad \gamma_k \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1), \quad \alpha \sim \mathrm{Normal}(-1.8, 1.5^2)$$ ::: {.note} A Normal(0, 0.5²) prior on the log OR gives 95% prior probability to ORs between 0.38 and 2.7 per 10 µg/m³. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r fit <- brms::brm( asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex, family = bernoulli, data = cohort, prior = c(prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b, coef = "Ino2_modeledD10"), prior(normal(0, 1), class = b), prior(normal(-1.8, 1.5), class = Intercept))) ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#bReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): the same posterior by normal approximation, in base R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- model.matrix(~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex, data = cohort) y <- cohort$asthma prior_sd <- c(1.5, 0.5, rep(1, ncol(X) - 2)); prior_mean <- c(-1.8, rep(0, ncol(X) - 1)) neg_log_post <- function(b) { eta <- X %*% b -sum(y * eta - log1p(exp(eta))) + sum((b - prior_mean)^2 / (2 * prior_sd^2)) } opt <- optim(rep(0, ncol(X)), neg_log_post, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE) post_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(opt$hessian))) exp(opt$par[2] + c(median = 0, low = -1.96, high = 1.96) * post_sd[2]) # OR per 10 ug/m3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> median low high #> 1.0533092 0.9474967 1.1709386 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional, not run when the site builds): the full brms model"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- brms::brm( asthma ~ I(no2_modeled / 10) + ses + green + parent_smoke + sex, family = bernoulli, data = cohort, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 22, prior = c(brms::prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b, coef = "Ino2_modeledD10"), brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b), brms::prior(normal(-1.8, 1.5), class = Intercept))) summary(fit) draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit) mean(exp(draws$b_Ino2_modeledD10) > 1) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gelman2008weakly propose weakly informative priors for logistic regression; @greenland2007bayesian on Bayesian regression in epidemiology; @burkner2017brms describes brms. ::: ## 22.2 Answering questions with posterior draws {#s2} Once you have posterior draws, every question is a computation on them. What is the probability that the odds ratio exceeds 1? That it exceeds 1.1? And, combining with Lesson 12, how many asthma cases per 1,000 children would a 10 µg/m³ reduction prevent? For that, g-computation is run once for every draw, giving a full posterior for the causal quantity. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$P(OR > c \mid y) \approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_s 1\{e^{10\beta^{(s)}} > c\}$$ $$\Delta^{(s)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\Big[\pi_i^{(s)}(x_i) - \pi_i^{(s)}(x_i - 10)\Big]$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit) mean(exp(draws$b_Ino2_modeledD10) > 1.1) # g-computation on every draw p_obs <- brms::posterior_epred(fit) p_int <- brms::posterior_epred(fit, newdata = mutate(cohort, no2_modeled = no2_modeled - 10)) cases_prevented <- 1000 * rowMeans(p_obs - p_int) quantile(cases_prevented, c(.025, .5, .975)) ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#qReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gelman2020regression on computing with posterior simulations; @kruschke2015doing on posterior probabilities of meaningful effects; @hernan2020causal on combining outcome models with standardization. ::: ## 22.3 Posterior predictive checks {#s3} Does the model reproduce the data? A **posterior predictive check** simulates new datasets from the fitted model, one per posterior draw, and compares them with the real data. Here the data are daily visits by Old Town residents aged 65+. A Poisson model with only an intercept, a Poisson model with season and day of week, and a negative binomial model are checked against the observed distribution and its variance. ```{=html}
observed20 replicated datasets
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$y^{\text{rep}(s)} \sim p(y \mid \theta^{(s)}), \qquad p_B = P\big(T(y^{\text{rep}}) \ge T(y) \mid y\big)$$ ::: {.note} $T$ = a test statistic, here the variance-to-mean ratio. $p_B$ near 0 or 1 signals misfit. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r brms::pp_check(fit, ndraws = 20) brms::pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = \(y) var(y) / mean(y)) # switch the likelihood: brms::brm(..., family = negbinomial) ``` :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Bayesian preview"} Posterior predictive checks ask whether the model could have produced the data. They don't choose between models. For that, Lesson 23 compares models by their out-of-sample predictive accuracy (LOO) and by Bayes factors, and shows when those two disagree. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gabry2019visualization on posterior predictive checks; @gelman2013bayesian on model checking with replicated data; @verhoef2007quasi on choosing between quasi-Poisson and negative binomial models. ::: ## 22.4 Reporting a Bayesian analysis {#s4} A Bayesian result is only interpretable alongside the choices that produced it. Reporting guidelines ask for the following, which together let a reader judge and reproduce the analysis: - the model, written out, and the reason for each prior, with a prior predictive check where helpful; - the software, sampler settings (chains, iterations, warm-up) and convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample sizes, any divergences); - posterior summaries: medians and credible intervals, and posterior probabilities for the questions of interest; - posterior predictive checks of fit; - a sensitivity analysis under alternative reasonable priors; - the data and code. ::::: {.triad} :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#rReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @kruschke2021bayesian set out the Bayesian analysis reporting guidelines; @gelman2020bayesian describe the full Bayesian workflow; @spiegelhalter2004bayesian on reporting Bayesian analyses in health research. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - Bayesian GLMs use the same model equations as Lesson 8, plus priors on the coefficients. - Priors on log odds ratios are easiest to set by thinking about plausible odds ratios; weakly informative priors rule out absurd values. - With much data the posterior matches the frequentist fit; with little data the prior matters, and its choice must be justified. - Posterior draws answer any question, including probabilities of meaningful effects and causal contrasts by g-computation. - Posterior predictive checks reveal misfit such as overdispersion; switch the likelihood when they fail. ```{=html}
